result.note: Tests the AMCA engine race (Reliance–Rolls-Royce vs Safran–GTRE), Tejas engine dependence on GE, and the August 2026 loitering munitions contracts.

questions.prompt: Consider the following statements about engine development for India's Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA), as of August 2026:
items: In August 2026, Reliance and Rolls-Royce signed a contract to build the engine for the AMCA.
France's Safran has proposed a joint venture with the Gas Turbine Research Establishment (GTRE) to develop a higher-thrust engine for later versions of the AMCA.
The Centre opened the AMCA programme to private firms in 2025.
questions.ask: Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explain: The Reliance–Rolls-Royce announcement of 14 August 2026 was only a statement of intent, with no contract signed and no money or ownership split disclosed. The AMCA is India's planned fifth-generation stealth jet, with a prototype due around 2028.
questions.source: The August 14 announcement is a statement of intent, with no contract signed yet.

questions.prompt: As of August 2026, India's Tejas fighter relies on engines supplied by which company?
questions.explain: Decades of Indian effort to build a high-thrust jet engine have fallen short, so even the Tejas depends on General Electric (GE) engines. This gap is why the AMCA engine contest between Reliance–Rolls-Royce and Safran–GTRE matters.
questions.source: India builds airframes, missiles, and radar, but decades of effort to produce a high-thrust jet engine have fallen short, leaving even the current Tejas fighter reliant on engines from General Electric (GE).

questions.prompt: In August 2026, India signed contracts worth INR 1,577 crore with Tata Advanced Systems and NIBE for the Army under Atmanirbhar Bharat rules. What were these contracts for?
questions.explain: Loitering munitions are drones that hover over a battlefield before diving into a target. Separately, the Ministry of Defence floated a INR 1 trillion tender to replace its ageing Soviet-era airlifters.
questions.source: On the same day, India inked INR 1,577 crore (USD 165 million) in contracts with Tata Advanced Systems and NIBE for loitering munitions, drones that hover over a battlefield before diving into a target, for the Army under its Atmanirbhar Bharat (self-reliant India) rules.
